title: ICE Has Been Dumping Protester Photos Into a Palantir Database
gist: A partially unsealed court filing in a proposed class action in Maine alleges a DHS agent logged ICE observers' photos, plates and personal data in the Palantir-built Investigative Case Management database, whose records can feed border lookouts. DHS calls the case meritless; the article also details Palantir's multi-year ICM contracts worth roughly $96 million plus nearly $30 million for ImmigrationOS.

insights.claim: A newly partially unsealed filing alleges DHS built dossiers on ICE observers, including photos and license plates, in the Palantir-built Investigative Case Management database.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Reputational and political risk for Palantir's government franchise as its tools are tied to alleged surveillance of citizens.
insights.locator: An explosive and newly partially unsealed

insights.claim: One agent allegedly created ICM records on at least six observers (the government says eight), labeled two filmed people 'Threat to Law Enforcement, Professional Protestor,' and sent photos to a CBP officer for facial recognition via the Mobile Query app.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Facial recognition plus case-management data fusion is the operational use of AI-enabled surveillance stacks that vendors enable.
insights.locator: According to the filings, J.C. created ICM records

insights.claim: ICM automatically shares agent-created subject records with CBP's TECS system, where they act as lookout records for border screening, per a 2016 DHS privacy assessment.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: A record created locally can propagate into border screening, a mechanism that raises legal exposure for the system's builders and users.
insights.locator: According to a 2016 DHS privacy assessment

insights.claim: One observer was allegedly flagged for secondary inspection at the border any time she crosses until at least January 2027.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Concrete downstream harm gives plaintiffs a stronger standing and damages narrative.

insights.claim: ICE awarded Palantir the contract to build ICM in 2014 on its Gotham software, then in 2022 a five-year support contract initially worth up to about $96 million, and added nearly $30 million in 2025 to develop a platform called ImmigrationOS.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Palantir has a decade-long, expanding revenue stream from ICE, but with growing litigation and headline exposure.
insights.locator: ICM is the system used by HSI agents

insights.claim: Palantir did not respond to requests for comment, and DHS calls the lawsuit meritless and based on 'the lie that there is a database of domestic terrorists run by DHS.'
insights.speaker: DHS spokesperson
insights.so_what: The government denies the characterisation, so outcomes hinge on court rulings on the motion to dismiss.
insights.quote: the underlying lawsuit is based on the lie that there is a database of ‘domestic terrorists’ run by DHS
insights.locator: A spokesperson for DHS calls the case

insights.claim: The proposed class action by four observers over 'Operation Catch of the Day', a January 2026 Maine enforcement surge, was filed under seal in September and made public in redacted form, based largely on government documents and agent depositions.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Discovery in civil suits is surfacing details of the surveillance stack, a recurring source of event risk for contractors.
insights.locator: The filing focuses on agents’ conduct

insights.claim: Former acting ICE director Todd Lyons wrote in April that ICE does not maintain a database of US citizens protesting, which plaintiffs' filing allegedly contradicts.
insights.speaker: Todd Lyons
insights.so_what: A gap between official statements and discovery documents raises oversight and congressional-inquiry risk.
insights.quote: does not maintain any kind of database of U.S. citizens protesting ICE activities
insights.locator: Todd Lyons, the former acting director

insights.claim: The government's motion to dismiss argues these were isolated incidents prohibited by DHS policy and that the agent made records on people he believed were potential threats, without nominating anyone to a terrorist watchlist.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: An 'isolated incident' defence limits systemic liability; watch the court's ruling.
insights.locator: The government’s motion to dismiss argues

insights.claim: Two observers stopped all ICE observation after an agent's phone call warning about a domestic terrorism watchlist, which plaintiffs cite as a First Amendment chilling effect.
insights.speaker: Maddy Varner
insights.so_what: Demonstrated chilling effect is central to the plaintiffs' relief request, including archiving records and barring use of collected data.
